lessons.title: Lesson 1: Reading a tape measure and adding fractions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read a tape measure to the nearest 1/16 inch and add or subtract two lengths.
This lesson builds toward: Given a tape measure and objects at home, you will read measurements to the nearest 1/16 inch and add or subtract fractional lengths, getting at least 4 of 5 right, with the work shown.
Carpentry runs on the tape measure. Each inch is split into 16 small spaces. The longest line in the middle of the inch is 1/2. The next longest lines are 1/4 and 3/4. Then come the eighths, and the shortest lines are sixteenths.
To read a length, find the last whole inch, then count the small lines past it. Ten sixteenths past 5 inches is 5-10/16, which you simplify to 5-5/8. Many tapes also mark every 16 inches in a different color, because that is a common stud spacing.
The metal hook at the end slides a little on purpose. It moves out when you hook the end of a board and in when you push against a wall, so both readings are true. Never bend it straight or file it.
To add fractions, make the bottom numbers match. 5-3/8 + 2-7/16 is 5-6/16 + 2-7/16 = 7-13/16. To subtract from a whole number, borrow one inch: 10 - 3-5/8 is 9-8/8 - 3-5/8 = 6-3/8. Measure twice, cut once.
Step by step:
- Hook the tape on the end of the board or push it flat against the wall.
- Find the last whole inch before the end.
- Count the sixteenth lines past that inch.
- Simplify the fraction (8/16 = 1/2, 4/16 = 1/4, 2/16 = 1/8).
- Write it down right away and measure again before you mark.
Words to know:
- Fraction: a part of a whole inch, such as 1/2, 3/8 or 5/16.
- Sixteenth: 1/16 inch, the smallest mark on most carpenter's tapes.
- Hook: the metal tab at the end of a tape; it slides so inside and outside readings are both correct.
- Simplify: write a fraction with smaller numbers that mean the same, like 10/16 = 5/8.
Try it now: Measure five things at home (a door width, a book, a shelf, a box, a table edge) to the nearest 1/16 inch and write each one down. Then add two of them and subtract the shorter from the longer, showing your work. Keep this page for your starter packet.
You can now read a tape measure to the nearest 1/16 inch and add or subtract lengths with fractions.

check.q: The tape shows 6 whole inches and 12 sixteenths past it. What is the length?
check.why: 12/16 simplifies to 3/4, so the length is 6-3/4 inches.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Lumber, sheet goods and fasteners
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the right board, sheet or fastener for a job and give its actual size.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple building job, you will choose the lumber, sheet goods and fasteners for it and give their actual sizes, with the right material and the actual size for at least 4 of 5 items.
Lumber is sold by a nominal size, the name, which is bigger than the actual size. A 2x4 is really about 1-1/2 by 3-1/2 inches. A 2x6 is about 1-1/2 by 5-1/2. A 1x10 is about 3/4 by 9-1/4. Always plan with the actual size, or your project will not fit.
Sheet goods come in 4-by-8-foot sheets. Plywood is thin layers of wood glued crosswise; OSB is pressed wood strands. Both cover floors, walls and roofs. Pressure-treated lumber has chemicals that resist rot and bugs, so it is used outdoors and touching concrete or the ground. Wear gloves and a dust mask when you cut it, and never burn the scraps.
Nails are sized by penny (written d). A 16d common nail, about 3-1/2 inches long, is a standard framing nail. Screws hold better and come out more easily; drill a small pilot hole near a board's end so it does not split. Outdoors, use coated or stainless fasteners so they do not rust.
Sight down a board before you use it. Most boards have a slight curve along the edge, called the crown. In floor joists and rafters the crown goes up, so the weight pushes it flat.
Words to know:
- Nominal size: the name size of lumber, like 2x4, which is bigger than its real size.
- Actual size: the real measured size, like 1-1/2 by 3-1/2 inches for a 2x4.
- Plywood and OSB: 4-by-8-foot sheets for floors, walls and roofs; plywood is glued layers, OSB is pressed wood strands.
- Pressure-treated: lumber with chemicals that resist rot and insects, used outdoors and near the ground.
- Penny (d): the size system for nails; a 16d common nail is about 3-1/2 inches long.
- Crown: the slight upward curve along a board's edge.
Try it now: At a store, online lumber page or in your home, find one board and one sheet. Write the nominal size, then the actual size. Then pick a fastener for each of these jobs and write why: framing a wall, a deck outdoors, a shelf near the end of a board.
You can now tell nominal from actual lumber sizes and choose boards, sheets and fasteners that fit the job.

check.q: You stack three 2x4s flat. About how thick is the stack?
check.why: A 2x4 is really about 1-1/2 inches thick, and 3 x 1-1/2 = 4-1/2 inches.

check.q: Which lumber do you use for a post that touches the ground outdoors?
check.why: Pressure-treated lumber resists rot and insects, which ground contact brings.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tool and ladder safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the protective gear and pre-use checks for a circular saw, a nail gun and a ladder.
This lesson builds toward: Before using a saw, nail gun or ladder, you will list the safety checks and protective equipment for the tool, naming the protective gear and at least four checks for each tool.
Carpentry injuries often come from saws, nail guns, falls and lifting. Every time, wear safety glasses, hearing protection around loud tools, work boots and, on a jobsite, a hard hat. Wear a dust mask when cutting makes dust. No loose sleeves, jewelry or long hair near a blade. If you are under 18, federal rules bar most power-saw and woodworking-machine work on the job; apprentices and student-learners 16 and older in approved programs have a limited exception.
Before using a circular saw: check the cord and plug or the battery, make sure the blade guard snaps back on its own, use a sharp blade made for the material, and clamp the work so it cannot move. Unplug the saw or take the battery out before you change a blade. Stand to the side of the cut line, keep both hands away from it, and let the blade stop before you lift the saw. A blade that binds can kick the saw back at you.
Nail guns: keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready, never point one at anyone, and disconnect the air or battery to clear a jam. A tool with a single-shot (sequential) trigger is safer for beginners.
Ladders (from OSHA's ladder safety card): inspect it first, keep three points of contact, face the ladder, set the base out about 1 foot for every 4 feet of height to the top support, extend it at least 3 feet above a landing, and do not stand on the top step unless it is made for that. Watch for power lines, especially with a metal ladder.
Step by step:
- Put on safety glasses, hearing protection and boots.
- Check the cord, plug or battery and the guard.
- Clamp the work.
- Unplug or remove the battery before changing a blade or clearing a jam.
- Set and check the ladder before you climb.
Words to know:
- PPE: personal protective equipment: safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves, boots, hard hat.
- Blade guard: the cover that springs back over a saw blade when the cut ends.
- Kickback: when a blade binds and the saw jumps back toward the user.
- Three points of contact: two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, on the ladder at all times.
Official sources:
- OSHA QuickCard: Portable Ladder Safety
- U.S. Department of Labor: Child labor rules for non-farm jobs (Fact Sheet 43)
Try it now: Write a pre-use safety checklist on a card for a circular saw (at least four checks and the gear you wear) and one for an extension ladder (at least four checks). If you have a ladder at home, do only the inspection and the 1-in-4 setup check; do not use a power saw at home without training. Keep the card for your starter packet.
You can now list the gear and checks before using a saw, a nail gun or a ladder, and know that cutting is learned in person with a qualified instructor.

check.q: You need to change the blade on a corded circular saw. What do you do first?
options: Ask someone to hold the guard open
check.why: Unplugging (or removing the battery) means the saw cannot start while your hands are near the blade.

check.q: The top support is 12 feet up a wall. About how far out does the ladder base go?
check.why: OSHA's rule is about 1 foot out for every 4 feet up: 12 / 4 = 3 feet.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading a plan and laying out a stud wall
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Lay out an 8-foot stud wall at 16 inches on center and count the studs and plates.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple wall plan, you will lay out a stud wall at 16 inches on center and count the studs and plates, with every stud mark within 1/16 inch and the right count.
A plan is a drawing to scale. On many house plans, 1/4 inch on paper equals 1 foot in real life. A floor plan looks down from above; an elevation shows a wall from the side. Lengths are written in feet and inches, such as 12'-6" (12 feet 6 inches). Never measure a printed plan with a ruler to get a size; use the written dimensions or ask.
A basic wall frame has a bottom plate, a top plate (often doubled), and studs standing between them. Studs are usually set 16 inches on center (o.c.), which means 16 inches from the center of one stud to the center of the next. Some walls use 24 inches o.c.; follow the plan.
To lay out: lay the bottom and top plates side by side, measure from one end, and mark both at once. Mark the first stud at the end, then marks at 16, 32, 48, 64, 80 inches. Many carpenters mark 3/4 inch before each line (15-1/4, 31-1/4 and so on) and put an X on the side where the stud goes, so the edges of 4-foot sheets land on stud centers. Put a last stud at the far end.
Count studs: wall length in inches divided by the spacing, plus one. An 8-foot wall is 96 inches; 96 / 16 = 6 spaces, so 7 studs. Corners, doors and windows need extra studs; the plan or your supervisor shows those.
Step by step:
- Read the wall length and stud spacing on the plan.
- Lay the top and bottom plates side by side, ends even.
- Mark both plates together from the same end.
- Mark an X where each stud goes, and a stud at each end.
- Count: length / spacing + 1, plus any extras the plan shows.
Words to know:
- Scale: how a drawing's size relates to real size, such as 1/4 inch = 1 foot.
- Floor plan and elevation: a floor plan looks down from above; an elevation shows one side of a wall or building.
- Plate: the flat board at the bottom or top of a wall that the studs stand on and hold up.
- Stud: a vertical board in a wall frame, often a 2x4 or 2x6.
- On center (o.c.): measured from the center of one stud to the center of the next.
Try it now: On paper (or on a long strip of cardboard taped out to 96 inches if you have room), draw an 8-foot wall. Mark the bottom plate at 16 inches on center from the left end, put an X where each stud goes, and write how many studs and plates you need. Check every mark with your tape. Keep it for your starter packet.
You can now read a simple wall plan and lay out studs at 16 inches on center with the right count.

check.q: What does 16 inches on center mean?
options: 16 inches between the edges of two studs
16 inches from the center of one stud to the center of the next
check.why: On center is measured center to center, so every stud lands at the same spacing.

check.q: How many studs does a 12-foot wall need at 16 inches on center, with no doors or windows?
check.why: 12 feet is 144 inches; 144 / 16 = 9 spaces, plus 1 = 10 studs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a cut list
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a cut list for a small project with actual sizes, kerf allowance and boards to buy.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small project drawing, you will write a cut list with actual sizes, saw-kerf allowance and the number of boards to buy, so every part fits on the boards listed.
A cut list is a table of every piece you need: the part name, how many, the material, and the exact length and width. It saves wood, money and trips to the store, and on a jobsite it lets a helper cut while the lead carpenter builds.
Use actual sizes. Example: a shelf 24 inches wide overall, made of 1x10. The two sides are 3/4 inch thick each, so the shelf board between them is 24 - 3/4 - 3/4 = 22-1/2 inches long.
Each saw cut turns a strip of wood into dust. That strip is the kerf, about 1/8 inch for many blades. Add one kerf for every cut when you plan how many pieces fit on a board.
Then plan the boards. From one 8-foot (96-inch) 1x10: two sides at 30 inches and one shelf at 22-1/2 inches use 82-1/2 inches, plus 3 kerfs (3/8 inch) is 82-7/8 inches, leaving about 13 inches of scrap. Boards are not always perfectly square or exactly 96 inches, so trim the factory end first and buy a little extra.
Step by step:
- List every part with its name and how many.
- Work out each length and width from actual sizes.
- Sort the parts by material.
- Fit the parts onto standard board lengths, adding one kerf per cut.
- Write how many boards to buy, plus a little extra.
Words to know:
- Cut list: a table of every piece to cut, with how many, the material and the sizes.
- Kerf: the width of wood a saw blade removes in one cut, often about 1/8 inch.
- Scrap: the leftover wood after you cut all your parts.
Try it now: Sketch a small shelf or planter box with its overall sizes. Write a cut list (part, how many, material, length, width) using actual board sizes. Then fit the parts onto 8-foot boards with 1/8 inch per cut and write how many boards to buy. Keep it for your starter packet.
You can now write a cut list from a small drawing and work out how many boards to buy.

check.q: A box is 18 inches wide overall with 3/4-inch sides. How long is the bottom board that fits between the sides?
Why do you add about 1/8 inch for each cut?
options: Boards are always longer than sold
The saw blade turns that much wood into dust
check.why: The kerf is the wood the blade removes, so the pieces need that space on the board.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your path: apprenticeship, NCCER and your first job
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find two carpentry apprenticeship or training programs and write a dated plan to apply.
This lesson builds toward: Using official websites for your area, you will write a dated plan to apply to two carpentry apprenticeship or training programs, with real programs, their requirements and a date for every step.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says carpenters usually learn on the job or in an apprenticeship, often sponsored by unions and contractor associations. Each year of an apprenticeship mixes technical classes with paid work. A high school diploma or equivalent is typically required. Look up pay and outlook on the BLS page, not in ads.
Find programs on apprenticeship.gov: the Apprenticeship Finder lists openings by career and place, and the Partner Finder shows sponsors accepting new apprentices. Also ask American Job Centers, community colleges, union training centers, Helmets to Hardhats (for veterans) and reentry pre-apprenticeship programs.
NCCER is a national construction training organization. Its carpentry curriculum starts with General Carpentry (with topics such as building materials and fasteners, construction plans, site and building layout, floors, walls, roof framing and stairs). NCCER certification requires passing a written assessment and a hands-on performance verification. Check nccer.org for where to train and test near you.
Many employers also ask for an OSHA 10-hour construction card. Running your own carpentry or contracting business may need a state or local license; employees usually work under the contractor's. Check your state's contractor licensing board. Under 18? Federal rules limit power-saw and roofing work; check dol.gov/youthrules.
Step by step:
- Read the BLS carpenters page for training and outlook.
- Search apprenticeship.gov for carpentry near you; pick two programs.
- Write each program's requirements and application dates.
- Gather documents: ID, diploma or GED, and anything else listed.
- Put a date on every step and a reminder in your phone.
Words to know:
- Apprenticeship: a paid job with classes, where you learn a trade from experienced workers.
- Pre-apprenticeship: a short program that teaches math, tools, safety and job skills to help you get into an apprenticeship.
- NCCER: the National Center for Construction Education and Research, which writes construction training and gives credentials.
- Performance verification: a hands-on test where an evaluator watches you do real tasks.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Carpenters (Occupational Outlook Handbook)
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Finder
- NCCER: Carpentry
- NCCER: Industry-recognized credentials
- U.S. Department of Labor: YouthRules
Try it now: Use apprenticeship.gov and the other places in this lesson to find two carpentry programs near you. For each, write the name, the requirements, how to apply and the deadline. Then write your plan with a date for every step: documents, math practice, OSHA 10, applying and following up. Keep it for your starter packet.
You can now find carpentry programs on official websites and follow a dated plan to apply.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Accurate measuring Fewer than 4 of 5 readings are right to 1/16 inch, or the fraction math has no work shown. At least 4 of 5 readings are right to 1/16 inch, and the sum and difference are right with the work shown. All five readings are right, every fraction is simplified, and the learner can explain the sliding hook. Safety checklist Missing protective gear, or fewer than four checks for the saw or the ladder. Names the gear and at least four checks each for the circular saw and the extension ladder, including unplugging and the 1-in-4 setup. Also covers kickback, power lines and three points of contact, and says the saw is learned with an instructor. Wall layout Stud marks are off by more than 1/16 inch, or the stud count is wrong. Plates marked at 16 inches on center from one end, an X on each stud, and the right count (7 studs for 8 feet). Also shows the 3/4-inch offset for sheet edges and notes extra studs for corners or openings. Cut list Uses nominal sizes, leaves out the kerf, or parts do not fit the boards listed. Every part with count, material and actual size; kerf added; all parts fit on the boards to buy. Also shows the scrap left on each board and a little extra for trimming. Materials chosen Board or fastener does not fit the job (for example untreated wood touching the ground). Lumber and fasteners fit the project, with actual sizes written. Explains why each choice fits, such as outdoor-rated fasteners or crown direction. Dated plan from official sources Steps have no dates, or programs and rules come from ads or posts. Two real programs with requirements and deadlines from official sites, and a date for every step. Also names a backup program and a person or office to call with questions. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where do you look up carpenters' pay and job outlook?
check.why: BLS is the official U.S. source for pay and outlook, updated regularly.

check.q: What do you need to pass for an NCCER certification in a craft?
options: A written assessment and a hands-on performance verification
check.why: NCCER says certification requires passing both a written assessment and a performance verification.
